  that could also be scripted from the shell. Over the following years the
  project grew steadily through contributions from a community of developers,
  and the 1.x and 2.x releases added better color support, mouse handling, and
  more flexible key bindings. Configuration moved to a plain text file, usually
  named .tmux.conf, which people shared in their dotfile repositories and blog
  posts, turning personal setups into a kind of informal culture. Plugin
  managers followed, letting users install community extensions for status bars,
  session saving, and themes. Later releases introduced features such as popup
  windows and more advanced layout tools, which kept the project relevant as
  developers' workflows moved toward remote servers, containers, and
  long-running build or deployment jobs. Today tmux is packaged in nearly every
  major Linux distribution and is available on macOS and the BSDs, and it
  remains one of the most widely used command-line tools for keeping terminal
  work organized and persistent.
